blink.title: Blink to find what moves
blink.body: SPHEREx photographs the whole sky again and again. Flip between two dates: stars stay put, but nearby stars, asteroids and comets jump. SPHEREx pixels are big, so most jumps are under one pixel — the crosshair shows where to look.

colours.title: 102 colours you can’t see
colours.body: SPHEREx sees infrared light, from 0.75 to 5 micrometres, in six groups called D1 to D6. We paint them with false colours so your eyes can tell them apart. Some cold objects only appear in D5 and D6.

mark.title: Mark the moving dot
mark.body: On a time-lapse, tap the dot on each frame. Your marks are compared with the predicted path and with what others marked. Many careful eyes measure motion better than one.

saturation.title: Too bright is a result too
saturation.body: Very bright stars overflow the detector, like a photo of the Sun. When that happens SkySwap says so instead of showing fake numbers.

longBaseline.timeline: When each photo was taken, 2010 to today
longBaseline.honest: WISE pixels are 2.75″ and SPHEREx pixels 6.15″, so SPHEREx frames look blurrier. Brightness is scaled per telescope; compare positions, not brightness. Empty corners on SPHEREx frames mean no data there.

kinds.mover: A moving object: it shows up in a different spot in each photo, like an asteroid crossing the sky.
kinds.residual: A leftover around a bright star. When photos taken at different times are compared, bright stars leave rings and smudges that don’t move.
kinds.single: A dot that shows up in only one photo — usually a tiny particle hitting the camera, not something in the sky.
kinds.trail: A streak across the photo — often a satellite or a camera glitch.
kinds.stationary: Something that stays in the same place in every photo.
kinds.orphan: A dot with no match in the other photos, so nothing shows it moving.

guesses.residual: a leftover around a bright star
guesses.orphan: a lone dot with no match

glitch.question: Looks like a camera glitch? (a streak, a smudge, or a dot that flashes once)

settings.dataBody: SkySwap shows real NASA SPHEREx images from public releases QR2 and QR3 (IRSA). Colours are false colours. The sky index lists {images} published images, so any spot can be opened. The first look at a deep-field spot, where SPHEREx returns again and again near the ecliptic poles, can take a few seconds while that part of the index downloads; after that it is kept in the browser. Data kit {version}.
settings.about: SkySwap is a non-commercial study prototype for the NASA Space Apps 2026 challenge “Planet X and SPHEREx”. It is not affiliated with NASA or Instagram.
